r: LANG 1260 applies knowledge of Asian geographies, histories, and contemporary politics to interdisciplinary synthesis, discussion, and written analysis of the intersections between domestic and global forces — colonization, nation-building, gender, migration. These are knowledge-work tasks: gathering and interpreting regional information, then communicating it in essays and class discussion. Task-exposure research finds programming and writing strongly positively associated with exposure, and this course's core deliverables sit squarely in that writing-and-synthesis category, so the underlying task is already AI-competent. What keeps the rating Low at 24 months is diffusion, not capability: Census BTOS data show only a minority of firms actively using AI in production workflows, and the course carries a GT-SS3 gtPathways designation plus a Global Diversity general-studies requirement that mandates enrollment regardless of task automatability. The instrumental need to take the course is intact for now.

By 2031, AI tools will competently draft the kind of comparative-region synthesis, historical contextualization, and thematic essay work this course assigns; observed-usage data already show writing and research tasks concentrated among the most common AI use cases, and that concentration should deepen as capability compounds on the reported four-to-seven-month task-horizon doubling trend. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this analysis weakens accordingly. What does not weaken is the institutional architecture: the course's GT-SS3 gtPathways designation and Global Diversity general-studies label are a statutory transfer requirement that does not turn on AI capability, so the rating rises only to Medium rather than tracking the underlying task exposure all the way up. Verification burden remains moderate — cultural and historical claims benefit from an instructor's disciplinary judgment — reinforcing that ceiling rather than lowering it further.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing fluent, well-sourced interdisciplinary synthesis on Asian politics, culture, and history essentially on demand, extending the erosion already visible at five years; task-exposure research's association between writing-heavy work and exposure points in the same direction over a longer horizon. The instrumental rationale for a student to personally develop this synthesis skill is substantially weakened in the central case. The rating nonetheless holds at Medium rather than rising further because the GT-SS3 gtPathways and Global Diversity general-studies mandate is a durable statutory transfer requirement unlikely to be relaxed within a decade absent a state policy change. Genuine uncertainty remains about how much instructors substitute AI-generated synthesis for original student work versus using it as a scaffold, which keeps confidence in the exact erosion pattern moderate rather than high.
LANG 1260.d: This course is an overview of Asia's diverse geographies, peoples, histories, and contemporary developments from an interdisciplinary perspective. Throughout the course, students investigate the intersection between domestic and global factors in shaping contemporary Asian experiences. Topics include Asia's dynamic cultures, rich philosophical, religious, and linguistic traditions, vibrant economies, and various types of political systems. Students also reflect on how issues such as colonization, nation- building, gender, and migration shape contemporary Asia and its many representations.

r: LANG 1300 teaches beginner professionals workplace-specific vocabulary, grammar, and case-study scenarios for multilingual careers in fields like public health, IT, and customer service — essentially transactional communicative competence for narrow professional contexts. This is close to the translation-and-basic-communication work that task-exposure research flags among the most exposed categories, since real-time machine translation already handles much routine workplace exchange. Observed-usage data show writing and communication assistance among the most common AI applications, and consumer-grade translation apps already approximate the LSP vocabulary this course drills. Unlike a GT-Pathways language sequence, this course carries no general-studies designation and no accreditation or licensure hook, so nothing but current diffusion protects it. At 24 months, adoption of real-time interpretation tools in professional settings is still uneven, so the instrumental need persists, but the erosion pathway is already visible and unusually direct for this course.

By 2031, real-time AI translation and interpretation will plausibly be embedded in the customer-service, health-care, and business contexts this course targets, directly substituting for the transactional professional communication it teaches; task-exposure research's positive association between exposure and both writing and interpreter-type tasks supports that trajectory. With no GT-Pathways designation, program-level accreditation floor, or foundational role protecting it — F4 and F5 both sit at the permissive end of the scale — nothing caps the rating below what the underlying task exposure implies. The course's in-class interactions retain some real-time interpersonal character, but that alone is not enough to hold the rating down once translation tools reach professional-grade fluency. The instrumental case for learning workplace phrases and grammar specifically to communicate across languages erodes substantially, moving the rating to High.

A decade out, the central case has ambient AI translation woven into professional workflows across the fields this course names — public health, IT, real estate, banking — making the instrumental case for memorizing workplace-specific vocabulary and grammar considerably weaker than it is today. Task-exposure research's classification of interpreter-type and communication tasks as highly exposed, combined with a capability trajectory that keeps compounding, supports a High rating with no institutional or foundational constraint to cap it. The hedge is genuine: professionals may still value personally speaking a client's language for trust and rapport in ways a translation earpiece does not replace, and diffusion into every listed industry is unlikely to be uniform. But absent a GT-Pathways lock or accreditation requirement, nothing in this course's design holds the rating below the underlying capability trend.
LANG 1300.d: In this course, students develop cultural awareness and learn how to navigate certain aspects of professions as they are practiced in other countries. The course is intended for beginner adult learners, specifically for professionals who plan to pursue careers in a multilingual setting. Students engage in a Language for Specific Purposes (LSP) approach, which includes in-class interactions, case studies, grammar, and vocabulary for professionals in a variety of fields (such as public health, information technology, real estate, human resources, customer service, business, banking, etc.). Coursework is rooted in concrete practices built around essential words, phrases, and structures that support basic yet effective communication in the workplace.

r: LANG 2400 introduces the professional fields of translation and interpreting directly, analyzing source texts across several languages and genres — scripture, literature, policy documents, marketing copy — through a Translation Studies lens, taught in English. The applied occupational tasks the course studies are translation and interpretation themselves, which task-exposure research names explicitly among the most-exposed occupations, alongside writers and tax preparers. Machine translation is already mature and widely deployed, and observed-usage data show writing and language tasks prominent among current AI applications, so the realized automatability of the core task is already high at 24 months. No general-studies designation, licensure hook, or foundational role constrains the rating. The course studies translation as a field rather than certifying interpreters for embodied real-time work, so the digital, text-based nature of its content leaves little institutional or embodiment protection.

By 2031, AI translation across the languages this course surveys — French, German, Italian, Korean, Russian, Spanish — will be fluent enough that the instrumental case for studying translation fundamentals as an entry to professional practice weakens further. Task-exposure research's explicit placement of translators and interpreters near the top of exposure rankings, combined with a capability trend compounding at roughly a four-to-seven-month task-horizon doubling pace, points toward continued erosion rather than a plateau. Verification burden is moderate rather than low: cultural and pragmatic nuance in literary or policy translation still benefits from trained judgment, but that residual does not rise to the adversarial, high-stakes character that would meaningfully dampen the rating. With no institutional lock or foundational role to cap it, the rating holds High, reflecting a course whose subject matter is unusually well-aligned with what AI already does competently.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing the great majority of routine translation and interpretation across written and increasingly spoken registers, leaving the course's foundational survey of the field's concepts less instrumentally necessary for entering professional translation work. This is one of the more direct matches in the catalog between a course's applied subject and the evidence base's explicit exposure ranking of translators and interpreters. The hedge concerns literary, diplomatic, and high-context translation, where cultural framing and ambiguity resolution may retain a longer human-judgment tail than routine commercial translation — genuine uncertainty rather than a confident prediction. But absent any general-studies designation, accreditation floor, or foundational scaffolding role, nothing in the course's institutional position holds the rating below High, and the underlying task trajectory is unusually well-documented in the evidence base.
LANG 2400.d: This course introduces new and advanced language learners alike to the professional fields of Translation and Interpreting within the broader language services industry. Basic concepts from the area of Translation Studies are introduced in a format that aligns with a culturally oriented approach in translation. Examples are drawn from a variety of source languages, including French, German, Italian, Korean, Russian, and Spanish among others. The analyzed texts represent a broad spectrum, and include excerpts from sacred scriptures, world literature, policy documents, marketing materials, lifestyle publications, and the translations of Harry Potter. The course is taught in English.

r: LANG 3050 applies knowledge of language families, migration history, and immigrant diaspora experience to interpretive synthesis and written analysis of heritage languages and cultures in the United States — a knowledge-and-writing course much like other interdisciplinary humanities offerings in the catalog. Task-exposure research finds writing and synthesis work strongly positively associated with exposure, and the course's deliverables — essays and discussion connecting historical migration patterns to contemporary identity — sit within that category. No general-studies designation, licensure hook, or program accreditation floor protects the course, and it plays no foundational role for later required coursework. At 24 months, however, diffusion of AI tools into routine coursework is still partial per Census BTOS adoption figures, and instructors have not yet restructured assignments around AI capability, so the instrumental erosion is real but not yet complete. The rating is Medium rather than Low or High.

By 2031, AI will fluently produce the kind of historical-cultural synthesis and heritage-language analysis this course assigns, and observed-usage data already show writing and research assistance among the most common AI applications — a concentration likely to deepen. With no GT-Pathways designation, accreditation floor, or foundational scaffolding role to cap it, little in the course's institutional position holds the rating down once the underlying task is well within AI's competence. The verification burden is moderate: claims about diaspora history and cultural identity benefit from disciplinary framing, but this is not an adversarial or safety-critical domain that would meaningfully dampen exposure. The rating rises to High, consistent with the pattern seen in other unprotected interdisciplinary writing courses in the catalog, where the same synthesis-and-exposition task profile drives the score once diffusion catches up to capability.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating scholarship-grade synthesis of migration history, language-family background, and diaspora identity essentially on demand, and this course's instrumental role in developing that synthesis skill is substantially eroded in that scenario. Task-exposure research's association between writing-heavy analytical work and exposure, combined with a fast-compounding capability trend, supports holding the rating at High rather than retreating toward Medium. The hedge is the standard ten-year one: forecasting this far out carries real uncertainty, and it is possible instructors redesign assignments around AI-assisted synthesis in ways that preserve a supervisory or curatorial role for students rather than eliminating the task outright. But with no institutional lock, licensure mandate, or foundational scaffolding role protecting the course, nothing in its design offers a floor beneath what the underlying task trajectory implies.
LANG 3050.d: Cultural Crossroads focuses on heritage languages and cultures in the USA. Students gain the cultural background necessary for insightful interaction with the rich diversity of heritage languages and cultures present in the United States. Main topics include the variety of language families, the historical and geo-political reasons for emigration, the establishment and treatment of immigrant diasporas, the role of differing social etiquette in cultural exchanges, the contributions of immigrants to their new country, and the importance of heritage languages in shaping identities, communities, and society.

r: This six-credit study-abroad course pairs interdisciplinary content — art, architecture, politics, literature, religion — with a five-week faculty-led immersion in Spain culminating in students physically walking the Camino de Santiago. The applied work is not primarily analytical output but an embodied, place-based experience: field trips, excursions, and the pilgrimage walk itself, undertaken for a personal transformation the course explicitly frames as the goal. Task-exposure frameworks place real-world physical activity and travel-based experiential learning among the least automatable categories, since no current or near-term AI system can substitute for walking an ancient route or visiting a site in person. No general-studies designation constrains the course institutionally, but embodiment alone is a strong protective factor here. At 24 months the instrumental need for a student to be physically present is untouched by any capability advance; the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI tools may well assist with trip planning, historical background research, or pre-departure content delivery for a course like this, and the interdisciplinary lecture material — art history, political and religious context — is the kind of synthesis task that task-exposure research classifies as exposed. But the defining applied task remains walking the route and engaging with excursions and field sites in person, which stays outside AI's reach regardless of how capable digital tools become; embodiment is the operative constraint, not capability. Verification burden is low here in a different sense — the personal, reflective nature of the experience is not adversarial or high-stakes — reinforcing rather than eroding the protection. The rating holds Low: gains in AI's ability to produce travel itineraries or historical summaries do not touch the instrumental core of the course.

A decade out, the analytical and pre-trip content components of this course — historical framing of the Camino, comparative study of European national identity — sit within a task category that, per task-exposure research, is increasingly well handled by AI, and it is plausible instructors lean more heavily on AI-assisted materials for that portion by 2036. That modest erosion nudges the rating from Low to Medium at this horizon. The physical pilgrimage and field excursions themselves remain the non-negotiable, embodied core the course is built around, and nothing in the capability trajectory substitutes for a student walking the route or standing at a historical site. The hedge is genuine: ten-year forecasts about how much course content shifts toward AI-assisted delivery are uncertain, but the embodied travel component anchors the floor regardless of how that shift plays out.
LANG 3950.d: This course is the foundational curriculum for a five- week study abroad experience in Spain. It is meant to be taught as part of an official MSU Denver faculty-led study abroad, and is not meant to be offered as regular curriculum during a normal semester on campus. This course may be taught in either English or Spanish (variable topic). In this course, students take an interdisciplinary approach to the study of European history. Students contribute to the joint experience of all students in the course by sharing the unique perspective that each individual brings to the examination of the material due to disciplinary formation and personal life experience. Course material examines the art, architecture, politics, economics, anthropology, literature, sociology, religion and historical events that led to the shaping of the Camino de Santiago itself and of Europe as a continent with many expressions of national identity. Field trips and excursions demonstrate how historical artifacts that were borne of intercultural interaction along the route have been preserved and integrated into the contemporary lives of Spaniards and all Europeans. Students then walk the ancient route themselves with the goal of undergoing and analyzing a personal transformation that offers new perspective into individual identity and the understanding of one's place in the larger historical world.

r: This internship places Modern Languages majors in professional field placements arranged through the Classroom to Career Hub, with requirements varying by department and specific applied tasks determined by the host site — commonly translation-adjacent work, language-support roles, or general professional duties where a language background is an asset. Because placement content varies, the applied work spans both AI-exposed categories (drafting, document review, correspondence) and more interpersonal on-site duties. Task-exposure research's finding that writing and language tasks are strongly exposed while in-person interpersonal work is not applies unevenly across this course depending on the specific internship. No general-studies designation or licensure mandate protects the course structurally, unlike a clinical placement in a regulated field. At 24 months, adoption of AI tools within typical internship host organizations is still uneven per diffusion data, so the instrumental value of the placement itself remains largely intact. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI assistance is likely to be routine within many of the professional settings hosting these internships, handling drafting, translation-adjacent tasks, and documentation work with the kind of productivity gains reported in professional-writing RCTs. Because this internship carries no licensure mandate, clinical-hour requirement, or accreditation floor — unlike, for instance, a nursing or teacher-preparation placement — nothing in the course's institutional design caps the rating as AI absorbs more of the routine tasks interns would otherwise perform. The residual value shifts toward interpersonal workplace competence and language-specific rapport-building, but the instrumental case for the internship as a vehicle for practicing now-automatable professional tasks weakens. The rating rises to High, reflecting the absence of any binding constraint analogous to the clock-hour and board-approval requirements that keep other field-placement courses in the catalog anchored at Low.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing much of the routine drafting, translation-support, and administrative work that a modern-languages internship placement would typically involve, substantially eroding the instrumental rationale for the placement as skills training in those specific tasks. Because the course lacks the licensure-gated, board-approved curriculum structure that protects clinical and teacher-preparation placements elsewhere in the catalog, no institutional floor holds the rating down. The hedge is that internship value increasingly shifts toward judgment, client relationships, and oversight of AI-assisted output rather than execution of routine tasks, and host organizations may restructure placements accordingly — a change in kind rather than a return of the original instrumental need. Confidence is moderate given how much depends on the specific, unspecified host-site duties, but the absence of any binding constraint supports a High rating in the central case.
LANG 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member within the major department, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: LANG 4960 develops competencies for teaching world languages — standards-based methods, classroom management, assessment design, differentiated instruction, and technology integration — paired with 12 hours of required classroom observation. The applied tasks include lesson and materials design, which task-exposure research would classify as writing-adjacent and moderately exposed, but the course exists within Colorado's educator-preparation pipeline: its corequisite field-experience pairing and its role in a state-approved licensure sequence mean completion is gated by a board-approved curriculum, not by task automatability. That licensure-gated structure is the strongest form of institutional lock the framework recognizes. At 24 months, even though AI can already draft sample lesson plans and assessment items competently, the requirement that teacher candidates complete this specific methods course as part of an approved preparation program is untouched. The rating is Low, driven entirely by the licensure constraint rather than task difficulty.

By 2031, AI-assisted lesson planning, item generation, and differentiated-materials design will plausibly be routine for practicing world-language teachers, and observed-usage data already show writing and instructional-content generation among common AI applications — a trend likely to deepen. That erodes the instrumental case for a candidate to personally master every method taught here, but Colorado's licensure framework does not relax on a single catalog cycle: the board-approved curriculum requirement that gates world-language teacher certification remains a hard constraint at this horizon. The rating therefore holds at Low rather than rising with the underlying task exposure, mirroring the Low-then-Low pattern seen elsewhere in the catalog for licensure-gated coursework whose credentialing requirement changes only slowly. The course's 12-hour observation component also retains a modest embodied, presence-dependent character that reinforces the floor.

A decade out, it becomes more plausible that licensure requirements around methods coursework loosen somewhat as AI-assisted planning tools become standard practice in K-12 language instruction, particularly if state boards revise preparation-program credit structures the way accreditation floors have shifted for other professions over long horizons. That plausibility, combined with continued erosion of the underlying lesson-design and assessment-development tasks per task-exposure research, supports a rise to Medium at ten years rather than an indefinite hold at Low. The rating does not rise further because Colorado's board-approval process for educator preparation is a genuinely durable institutional brake, and there is no strong central-case evidence that licensure-gated curricula move faster than a decade. Confidence in the exact timing of any such loosening is low; the direction is more defensible than the magnitude.
LANG 4960.d: Students develop competencies for teaching world languages. Course content includes methods and materials of standards-based instruction, classroom and instructional management, assessment strategies, designing lessons using multiple intelligences and differentiated instruction, using technology in instruction, and integration of other content areas in the teaching of world languages. Students are required to complete a minimum of 12 hours of observation in a variety of world language classrooms.

r: This field-based course places teacher candidates in a world-language classroom to design and implement content lessons and literacy strategies under a cooperating teacher's supervision, arranged through MSU Denver's Office of Clinical Experiences and Partnerships. The applied work is in-person instructional delivery with real K-12 students — precisely the embodied, real-time interpersonal category that task-exposure research identifies as low-exposure, in contrast to the writing and programming tasks that rank highest. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: Colorado educator licensure conditions certification on completion of a board-approved preparation program with mandated field hours, and no AI system can satisfy that clinical requirement on a candidate's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised in-person field experience is completely untouched by any advance in AI capability, because the operative barrier is regulatory and embodied, not informational. The rating is Low with high confidence.

AI-assisted lesson-planning and assessment tools will likely be common in the K-12 classrooms hosting these placements by 2031, and candidates will increasingly practice overseeing AI-generated materials rather than building every lesson from scratch. But the course's core purpose — developing a candidate's embodied competence managing and teaching live learners under supervision — is a formative, presence-dependent activity that automation does not perform, and the verification burden around working with minors keeps a knowledgeable human supervisor central regardless of tool sophistication. Colorado's licensure field-hour mandate does not relax within one or two catalog cycles; institutional brakes of this kind move on multi-year, board-driven timelines rather than tracking capability growth. The rating stays Low: what changes is the content candidates practice overseeing, not whether the supervised placement itself remains necessary.

Even under an aggressive central-case capability scenario for AI in K-12 instruction, the requirement that world-language teacher candidates accumulate supervised in-person field hours with real students is among the more durable constraints in the catalog, and there is no credible path to Colorado relaxing that clinical-hour mandate within a decade absent a fundamental restructuring of educator licensure. The embodied, interpersonal, real-time nature of managing a classroom of K-12 learners resists direct substitution regardless of how fluent AI-generated lesson content becomes. Genuine uncertainty exists about how heavily AI mediates the instructional materials candidates deliver during this placement, but the field-experience requirement itself — and the supervised competence it certifies — remains necessary in the central case. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the licensure and embodiment factors together.
LANG 4961.d: Students in this field-based course engage in opportunities to develop professional and pedagogical skills in a world language classroom. In coordination with the classroom teacher, teacher candidates design and implement content lessons and use content literacy strategies to improve both language acquisition and literacy skills. Students' field placement in schools is arranged by MSU Denver faculty, the Office of Clinical Experiences and Partnerships, and partner schools. Students must complete EDS 3170 and EDS 3240. This course is NOT intended as a beginning field experience. Students should take this course concurrently with LANG 4960.

r: This teaching-assistantship course has students assist a professor of record with designing and delivering world-languages coursework, participating in in-class sessions, and supporting the instructor's ongoing projects, including data collection and literature review. The applied tasks split between exposed knowledge work — literature review, materials preparation, data collection — and in-person classroom co-delivery, giving the course a mixed exposure profile. Task-exposure research's positive association between writing and research tasks and exposure covers the former; the latter retains more interpersonal, presence-dependent character. No general-studies designation or accreditation floor protects the course, and it plays no foundational role in the curriculum. At 24 months, AI tools already competently assist with literature summaries and data organization, but classroom co-delivery and instructor collaboration remain largely human activities in current practice, keeping the rating at Medium rather than lower or higher.

By 2031, AI-assisted literature review, data organization, and course-materials drafting will likely be routine for a role like this, consistent with observed-usage data showing research and writing assistance among the most common current AI applications — a share likely to grow. With no general-studies designation, accreditation floor, or foundational scaffolding role to cap the rating, the erosion in the knowledge-work portion of the assistantship's duties is not institutionally offset. The in-class co-delivery component retains some real-time interpersonal character, but that alone does not hold the rating at Medium once the bulk of the assistantship's documented tasks — literature review, data collection, materials support — are well within AI's competence. The rating rises to High, tracking the underlying task exposure now that near-term diffusion limits have loosened.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most of the literature-review, data-collection, and materials-preparation work this teaching assistantship is built around, substantially eroding the instrumental rationale for a student performing those tasks manually as career exploration. Task-exposure research's classification of research-support and writing tasks as highly exposed, combined with a fast-compounding capability trend, supports holding the rating at High. The hedge concerns the in-class collaborative and mentoring relationship with the professor of record, which may retain value as a professional-development experience even as the specific task content automates — a change in the assistantship's purpose rather than evidence against the rating. With no institutional lock or foundational role protecting the course, nothing in its design provides a floor below what the underlying task trajectory implies. Confidence is moderate given the description's genericness.
LANG 4980.d: This course is organized around the concepts of teaching world languages and surveying teaching methods that enhance student learning and promote successful outcomes. The student learns and applies strategies for teaching world languages in order to assist the professor of record with the design and delivery of world languages courses. The student plays an active role in delivering course content and applying best-practice methodologies to the organization of in-class sessions. The student also participates in teaching-related projects that the professor of record is working on during a particular semester. The student may assist with data collection, literature review, etc. This course promotes the acquisition of transferable skills that prepare the student for future professional opportunities in world languages teaching.
